l01.heard: Every 27 minutes someone in Goa is bitten by a dog.

l02.heard: In 2025 alone, that was 19,368 bite cases.

l03.heard: And when you find an injured animal on the road, who do you even call?

l04.heard: Every municipality runs its own helpline. Some close at 8:00 in the evening.

l05.heard: And last year, Canacona, Sanghalem, Valpoi and Mapsa held no sterilization camps at all.

l06.heard: Meet Paw SOS Goa. One WhatsApp number for every animal emergency in the state. No app to install.

l07.heard: Here it is working. You send a photo of the animal and your location.

l08.heard: Within seconds, Claude looks at the photo and replies, "How urgent it seems." And two or three safe things to do while you wait. It is guidance, never a diagnosis.

l09.heard: If someone else reports the same animal nearby, Pa SOS merges it into the same case. The team gets one alert, not two.

l10.heard: The nearest partner team gets the photo, a map link, and two buttons, accept or decline.

l11.heard: If nobody answers in time, the case moves on to the next team, and then to the Taluka officer. Nothing waits forever.

l12.heard: accepted, on site, resolved. And the person who reported it, hears every single step.

l13.heard: For officials, every case sits on one map with a full order trail and a suggestion for where the next sterilization camp is needed.

l14.heard: Under the hood, it is one Python service and one PostGIS database.

l15.heard: WhatsApp, Telegram, and this web demo all arrive as the same message. So they run the same logic.

l16.heard: One state machine owns every case and records every change. If the AI is slow, the case is rooted anyway. If a message fails to send, the case is never lost.

l17.heard: The teams in this demo are placeholders and the WhatsApp line is waiting on meta's business verification. But the whole loop works today.

l18.heard: This is PAWS SOS Goa. One number, every report heard.
